cells.tense: Right now you have both hands on what the whole picture asks for.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Among your people, find one arrangement that was right when you set it and isn't now. End it this week without explaining why, then watch what the people inside it do with the space.
cells.core:
You can hold the whole picture of something and still make one plain call inside it. What's out of balance gets its weight from you, then gets settled. The call doesn't fight the picture. You let a feeling finish before you put the pen down, and what leaves you is fair rather than argued.

Something you keep standing has outlived its use. You keep it because ending it costs the comfort of a thing you already got right. End it anyway, once, without stating a reason. Watch what the people inside it do with the space, and take the plainness of that for yourself. What was fair a year ago isn't waiting to become fair again.
cells.sheetLine: You see it whole and still call it fair.
cells.verb: Calling what's out of proportion fair, while feeling all of it
cells.place: standing back and seeing the whole shape of a thing at once

cells.tense: You are bracing for how a wound will read before it has happened.
cells.act: hold the weight as a builder holds stone
cells.ask: When the next sting lands between people, carry it a full day before deciding if it was fair. Feel the load without reaching for a verdict. Judge it tomorrow.
cells.core:
You can already see the whole pattern of a thing between people — where it started, who it lands on, whether it comes out even. So you settle it early, while the sting is still arriving. What you see is accurate. A sting needs its hour before it can hear a ruling.

Carry the next one for a day without deciding what it's for. Stones get lifted before anyone knows which wall they belong in. By morning the ruling will still be there, and shorter. The person it concerns will manage to hear it. Walk in already holding a sentence and the day feels like a trial nobody agreed to.
cells.sheetLine: You rule on feelings while they're still being felt.
cells.verb: Calling what's out of proportion fair, while feeling all of it

cells.tense: You once saw a fair way through it, and you stepped back from the door.
cells.act: put the inquiry on paper and follow it
cells.ask: Take one situation near you that's off balance. Lay the facts on paper, one after the other. Keep every feeling word off it. Read it back once.
cells.core:
Somewhere near you, things between people have gone out of proportion and you can see it plainly. You did what you did with that sight, and since then you've been standing at a door that's already behind you. The room keeps paying for it in small ways.

Nerve isn't required to set a sentence down. Take the unfair thing and lay out the facts on paper, one after the other, with no feeling adjectives on the page. Read it back once. The call is half-made in your own handwriting. Method here does what nerve won't: it starts the sight again, and fairness comes back in plain clothes.

cells.tense: The whole pattern is visible to you, and you talk like you're not the one seeing it.
cells.act: ask the question you do not know the answer to
cells.ask: During the next argument near you, let one person finish, then ask a question you truly don't know the answer to. Stay for the reply. Don't fix anything yet.
cells.core:
Things between the people near you stay level because you keep them that way — a word here, a weight set down there — and when you tell it, you stayed out of it. The balance has a keeper. The keeper's story is that of a bystander, while the people being kept level don't buy it.

Ask a real question first. In the next argument, let one person finish and put a question to them that you don't know the answer to, then stay for the reply. You'll hear the part you usually smooth over, and the work of keeping things level gets seen from inside by the one doing it. Nothing else changes, and the one who says they stayed out has just watched themselves step in.
